intro:
These exercises take memory profiling out of the realm of tool worship and put it on a fixed triage order: name the symptom precisely, measure allocation and retention together, correlate the memory curve with the workload curve, and only then commit to a diagnosis. The work moves from the cheapest possible instrument (a local clone or allocation counter) up through heap snapshots, reference-cycle inspection, and async backlog analysis, mirroring the chapter's claim that the most expensive optimization is the one made before the symptom is understood.

The through-line is that Rust's memory behavior is a consequence of ownership decisions you already control. A rising resident set can be allocation churn, retained heap, allocator fragmentation, a reference cycle, or an unbounded queue, and these have different fixes. The exercises train you to distinguish those cases with the smallest measurement that rules out the most wrong theories, then repair the design (borrow instead of clone, weaken a back-edge, bound a queue) rather than reaching for an allocator trick first.

exerciseSolutions.title: Match the symptom to the measurement
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Each symptom points at a different first measurement because each describes a different mechanism keeping bytes resident. The skill is to choose the measurement that fastest rules out the wrong theories, not to default to a full heap profiler.

Rising RSS after a burst that does not fall back down points first toward fragmentation or allocator retention. Before assuming a leak, measure the disagreement between live bytes (what your program logically holds, from a heap profiler or a global counter) and process RSS. If live bytes return to baseline while RSS stays high, the allocator is holding freed pages to satisfy the next request quickly. That is allocator behavior, not a leak; the right follow-up is allocator stats or an explicit trim, not a hunt for a missing drop.

Stable RSS but a rising task count points toward async backlog rather than a leak. Memory is flat, so nothing is being retained abnormally; the growing number is in-flight work. Measure task count and queue depth. This is an admission-control problem: producers outrun consumers, and the runtime accumulates tasks. The fix is a bound (semaphore or bounded channel), not allocator inspection.

Flat heap snapshots with a high allocation rate point toward churn rather than retained memory. Two successive snapshots show roughly the same live set, yet the allocator is busy. Measure allocation count and cloned bytes per request. Live data is not growing, so this is throughput cost from short-lived allocations (often deep clones), addressed by borrowing or reuse, not by leak hunting.

A graph of Rc nodes that never disappears points toward logical reachability and cycle inspection. Safe Rust never reads freed memory, but it does not promise that unneeded memory is freed. Inspect strong counts: if a subgraph's strong count never reaches zero after local work ends, a cycle still has owners. The repair is to make one back-edge non-owning (Weak) or to drop shared ownership entirely in favor of arena handles.
criteria: A distinct first measurement is chosen per symptom: RSS-vs-live for retention, task/queue count for backlog, allocation count for churn, strong-count inspection for cycles.
Retained memory (cycles, fragmentation) is separated from allocation churn (flat snapshots, high rate) explicitly.
Each diagnosis is gated on evidence; none is called a leak before a measurement distinguishes it from churn, backlog, or allocator retention.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find clone pressure in a sample workload
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the path with one question in mind: which operations create a second owner of the same allocation, and which copy underlying bytes into fresh heap. In safe Rust the word clone covers both, and only the second one drives memory growth.

When the route filter clones owned strings into an output list with route.to_string() (the shape in the chapter's clone-pressure counter, where each surviving route does out.push(route.to_string())), that is a deep clone: it allocates a new buffer and copies the bytes. The later formatting step, building another owned label per selected item with format!(...), is a second deep clone for the same reason. By contrast, an Arc::clone or Rc::clone on a shared handle creates another owner of one allocation and copies no bytes; that is cheap and is not the source of growth. So the two .to_string()/format! sites are the deep clones; any Arc::clone in the path is not.

The helper that only needed borrowed access is the route filter itself. Choosing which routes survive requires reading the strings (route.starts_with("/api/")), not owning them. It can take &[&str] and return Vec<&str>, borrowing for the lifetime of the input slice. The deep clone is forced only if a downstream stage must outlive the input. If the queued work genuinely outlives the request buffer, that is where ownership should become explicit: clone once at that boundary with a comment naming why, rather than cloning eagerly inside the filter where the data is still borrowable.

Before reaching for a whole-process heap profiler, add a local counter on the hot path: count clone events and sum cloned bytes (using the borrowed source length before conversion). That single comparative number tells you whether a refactor doubled the duplicated bytes per request, which is usually enough to pick the next target without a full trace.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The filter needs only borrowed access; defer ownership to the boundary that truly outlives the input.
criteria: At least one deep-clone site is identified correctly: route.to_string() and the per-item format! both allocate fresh buffers.
A borrowed-API repair is proposed: select_api returns Vec<&str> tied to the input lifetime instead of Vec<String>.
A local measurement is named: clone count and cloned-byte total computed from borrowed source lengths before conversion.

exerciseSolutions.title: Instrument clone pressure on purpose
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The goal is a narrow, comparative instrument that proves where deep-copy work happens, before committing to a heavier heap profiler. It follows the chapter's clone-pressure counter directly: filter, then clone, then count, with two separate numbers.

Keep clone events and cloned bytes as distinct counters. The count answers how many owned values this path produced; the byte total answers how heavy each one was. They describe different problems and can move independently: a refactor can hold the count flat while doubling the bytes, or fan out many tiny clones. Capture the byte size from the borrowed source length before conversion, so you are measuring the cost the path chose at the moment of choosing it.

Keep the instrumentation local to the hot path. A small &mut CloneStats threaded through one function is enough; do not promote it to a global allocator hook or a framework abstraction. The value is comparative, not absolute: you read it across a refactor or incident window to see what changed. The exact number on any single run matters far less than the delta between the suspect build and the baseline.

This is not a complete memory profile and is not meant to be one. It does not see allocations elsewhere, retention, or fragmentation; it answers exactly one question (how much deep-copy work did this path do) so it can point the next, heavier pass at the right subsystem. Delete it once the incident is resolved and the regression is confirmed fixed, because permanent micro-instrumentation accretes into noise; if the path is genuinely worth watching forever, graduate it to a real metric behind a feature flag rather than leaving the ad hoc counter in place.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Two separate counters, threaded locally; read the delta across a refactor, then delete.
criteria: Clone events and cloned bytes are counted explicitly as two separate fields on CloneStats.
The instrument stays local: a &mut CloneStats threaded through one hot-path function, not a global abstraction.
It is framed as comparative: a delta across a refactor window that guides the next profiling pass, not a whole-process trace.

exerciseSolutions.title: Diagnose an Rc cycle leak
exerciseSolutions.solution:
State the leak precisely in terms of strong ownership count, because the bug is not that Rust leaked; it is that the graph still has owners. Each Rc holds a strong count, and a value's destructor runs only when that count reaches zero. When the parent stores children as Rc<Node> and each child stores its parent as Rc<Node>, the two edges keep each other's strong count permanently above zero. After local work ends and the external handle drops, root's strong count does not fall to zero (the leaf still owns it), so neither node is freed. That is the logical leak: the memory is fully reachable by design and therefore never collected.

The key distinction is which edge owns lifetime and which edge only wants to look something up. The child-to-parent (back) edge is observational: a child needs to find its parent, but it should not keep its parent alive. The parent-to-child (forward) edge is owning: the tree's lifetime should follow the parent, and children should live as long as the parent holds them. So the forward edge stays Rc<Node> and the back-edge becomes Weak<Node>, exactly as in the chapter's rc-cycle example, where GoodNode stores parent: RefCell<Weak<GoodNode>> while keeping children as Rc.

With Weak, the back-edge no longer contributes to the strong count. To inspect the repair, print Rc::strong_count(&root) before and after dropping the external handle. In the strong-cycle build the count stays at two and the subgraph can never drop; in the Weak build it falls to zero when the last strong owner goes away, and the destructors run. Reading the parent goes through upgrade(), which returns None once the parent is gone, making the dangling case explicit instead of silently retained.

When shared ownership is not semantically real, the calmer design is arena handles: store nodes in a Vec or arena and represent edges as plain indices (NodeId). No reference counting, no cycle risk, no Weak upgrades; lifetime is the arena's, and a parent index is just data. That trades pointer-chasing convenience for an explicit ownership model and is usually the right call for tree- and graph-shaped data where no node truly owns another's lifetime.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Weak on the back-edge keeps the strong count at 1; the subgraph collects when the last owner drops.
criteria: The leak is explained as strong-count retention: mutual Rc edges hold each other's count above zero, so destructors never run.
The parent back-edge is replaced with Weak<Node>, matching the chapter's GoodNode shape, while the forward edge stays Rc.
An alternative is named: arena handles (NodeId indices) when no node semantically owns another's lifetime.
strong_count before/after is named as the signal to inspect across the repair.

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile async memory usage before calling it a leak
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Async memory growth usually traces to a boundedness failure, not a leak, so collect all three signals first: queue depth, task count, and payload size, tracked together. A genuine leak moves one of them in isolation; an admission problem moves several at once, and that pattern is what tells them apart. The chapter's sketch groups the four fields into one struct precisely so you read them as a set.

This pipeline has two boundedness failures. The unbounded channel lets the queue absorb the gap whenever the consumer falls behind, and every queued message keeps its payload alive; queue depth and resident bytes rise together. The spawn-per-input-item has no cap, so task count climbs with input rate, and each in-flight task pins its large owned payload across the awaits it holds. Both keep memory alive while every object remains perfectly reachable by design.

The boundary that wants a cap is the producer-to-consumer channel: replace the unbounded channel with a bounded one so the producer experiences backpressure and stalls instead of buffering without limit. The spawn boundary wants a concurrency cap: gate it with a semaphore so only N tasks run concurrently, which bounds both the task count and the number of simultaneously pinned payloads. The reason is the same in both places: an unbounded admission point converts a throughput mismatch into unbounded memory.

The payload-shape repair is to shrink or borrow the data before it crosses the spawn boundary. A large owned payload that survives several awaits is held for the whole task lifetime; extract only the fields the task needs, or pass an Arc of the shared part so many tasks reference one allocation instead of each owning a copy. After bounding the channel, capping concurrency, and shrinking the payload, watch queue depth, task count, and resident bytes: if they plateau, it was admission, not a leak. You would still suspect a true leak if, with all three caps in place and the input drained, live bytes do not return to baseline; at that point inspect retention (reference cycles, a non-evicting cache, an arena that never resets) rather than backlog.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Bound the channel, cap concurrency with a semaphore, and share the payload via Arc; then watch the three signals plateau.
criteria: At least one boundedness failure is identified: the unbounded channel and the uncapped spawn-per-item.
A concrete cap is proposed with a reason: bounded mpsc for backpressure and a Semaphore to bound concurrent tasks/payloads.
A payload-shape repair (Arc-share or extract needed fields before the spawn boundary) plus a confirming metric (queue depth, task count, and resident bytes plateauing) are named.
A condition for still suspecting a true leak is given: live bytes not returning to baseline after all caps are in place and input drained.

exerciseSolutions.title: Prepare a memory profiling checklist for a real service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The checklist's job is to force the team to rule out wrong theories quickly, in a fixed order, so it pairs allocator/heap signals with workload signals and ends in a concrete stop condition rather than a vibe. It mirrors the chapter's triage order: name the symptom, measure allocation and retention together, correlate with the workload curve, then diagnose.

First page of the investigation (collect together, not one at a time): process RSS; live bytes from a heap profiler or global counter; allocation count and rate; queue depth and queue age; task count; clone count and cloned bytes per request; cache size and hit rate. The point of putting them on one page is the correlation: RSS rising with live bytes flat means fragmentation or allocator retention; RSS flat with task count rising means backlog; live bytes rising with queue depth means an unbounded queue; high allocation rate with flat live bytes means churn. No single number diagnoses; the pattern across them does.

Named retention candidates to rule out explicitly: Rc or Arc cycles (inspect strong counts on the graph types; convert back-edges to Weak); unbounded queues or task floods (the async channel and spawn boundaries; add bounded channels and a semaphore); non-evicting caches (the read-mostly cache that only inserts; add a size or TTL bound); oversized or never-reset arenas (the parser's arena; confirm it resets per request and is sized to peak, not cumulative). Each candidate has a measurement that confirms or clears it before any code changes.

OS tools by platform, clustered by job (growth by callsite, resident-versus-logical disagreement, timeline correlation): on Linux, heaptrack or valgrind/massif for callsite growth, /proc/<pid>/status (VmRSS) plus jemalloc/tikv-jemalloc stats for resident-versus-logical, and perf or a metrics pipeline for the timeline. On macOS, Instruments (Allocations/Leaks) for callsites and the timeline, and vmmap/footprint for resident-versus-logical. On Windows, the VMMap and Heap tools (Sysinternals) or WPA/Windows Performance Recorder for callsites and timeline, and Task Manager/Performance Monitor working-set counters for resident. Pick the callsite tool for who allocated, the resident tool for fragmentation, and the timeline tool to align the memory curve with the workload curve.

Success condition (one concrete stop, not 'looks better'): after the fix and a repeat of the original burst, RSS returns to within an agreed margin of pre-burst baseline once the burst ends and the queue drains, and cloned bytes per request (or live bytes at steady state) are at or below the pre-regression number. Define it numerically before starting so a masked symptom (for example, RSS that merely grows slower) does not get mistaken for a resolved one.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: A one-page checklist: correlated first-page numbers, named retention candidates, per-OS tools, and a numeric stop condition.
criteria: Allocator/heap signals (RSS, live bytes, allocation count) are paired with workload signals (queue depth, queue age, task count, clone count).
At least three retention sources are named explicitly: Rc/Arc cycles, unbounded queues, non-evicting caches, oversized arenas.
At least one tool per platform is chosen: Linux (heaptrack/massif, /proc, jemalloc), macOS (Instruments, vmmap), Windows (VMMap/WPR, PerfMon).
One concrete numeric success condition is defined: RSS back to within a margin of baseline after the burst drains, plus cloned/live bytes at or below the pre-regression value.

labSolution.explanation:
The starter code returned Vec<String>, cloning every selected route through track_clone, which incremented the atomic counter once per output element. Two routes start with "/api/", so the original path reported two clones for two selected items: the clone count tracked the selected count exactly because every survivor was deep-copied.

The fix is an API-shape change, not an allocator trick. Choosing which routes survive requires only borrowed access (route.starts_with("/api/")), so hot_routes can take &[&'a str] and return Vec<&'a str>, where the lifetime 'a ties the output references to the input slice. Each surviving &str is pushed by value as a borrow of the existing string literal; no new heap buffer is allocated and track_clone is never called. The borrow checker proves this is sound: selected may not outlive routes, which is exactly the constraint that makes avoiding the clone safe.

At runtime, two routes match so selected.len() is 2, and because nothing in hot_routes calls track_clone, the CLONES counter stays at the value set by CLONES.store(0, ...), printing 0. The program therefore prints "selected = 2" then "clones = 0", matching the expected output. The deep clone returns only if a later stage must outlive the input buffer, in which case you would clone once at that boundary with a comment, rather than eagerly inside the filter.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a local clone counter often a good first memory-profiling tool?
reviewAnswers.answer: It is the cheapest instrument that distinguishes the most common cause of allocation churn in safe Rust, deep clones, from cheap reference-count clones, and it does so without a whole-process trace. Threaded as a small &mut counter through one hot path, it adds almost nothing and answers a single narrow question: how much deep-copy work did this path choose. Its value is comparative; reading the clone count and cloned-byte delta across a refactor or incident window proves whether one change doubled the duplicated bytes per request, which usually points at the next target directly. That lets you avoid rewriting the wrong subsystem before a heavier heap profiler is even warranted.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between allocation churn and retained live data?
reviewAnswers.answer: Allocation churn is how often and how many bytes the program asks the allocator for; retained live data is how much of what was allocated is still reachable and alive right now. Churn shows up as a high allocation rate with flat heap snapshots: the live set is roughly constant between snapshots even though the allocator is busy, which is a throughput cost usually fixed by borrowing or reuse. Retention shows up as live bytes that grow and do not return to baseline, which is a leak-shaped problem fixed by removing an owner (a cycle, an unbounded queue, a non-evicting cache). They are two separate numbers describing two different problems, and treating churn as a leak sends you hunting for a missing drop that does not exist.

reviewAnswers.question: Why can RSS stay high after the logical working set falls?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because RSS measures the pages the operating system has given the process, not the bytes the program logically holds, and when you free memory the allocator does not necessarily return those pages to the OS. Allocators typically retain freed pages to satisfy the next request quickly, so the resident set can stay high while live bytes have already dropped back to baseline. This gap between logical and resident memory is fragmentation or allocator retention, not a leak; the way to confirm it is to compare live bytes against RSS, and if live bytes returned but RSS did not, the allocator is holding the difference. The remedy is allocator-level (tuning or an explicit trim), not a search for unreachable objects.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are unbounded queues and task floods often memory bugs even when no object is unreachable?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because memory stays alive as long as something reachable owns it, and a growing backlog owns every item in it by design. When producers outrun consumers across an unbounded channel, the queue absorbs the difference and each queued message keeps its payload alive; when a service spawns a task per input without a cap, each in-flight task pins its payload across the awaits it holds. Nothing is unreachable, so a leak detector finds nothing, yet resident memory climbs with queue depth and task count. The fix is admission control, a bounded channel for backpressure and a semaphore to cap concurrency, not allocator inspection, and the tell is that several workload signals rise together rather than one in isolation.

reviewAnswers.question: What does Weak<T> repair that a strong Rc<T> or Arc<T> back-edge cannot?
reviewAnswers.answer: Weak<T> lets an edge observe a value without owning its lifetime, which is exactly what a back-edge in a parent/child or graph structure needs. A strong Rc or Arc back-edge contributes to the strong count, so a parent and child that both hold strong references to each other keep each other's count permanently above zero; their destructors never run and the subgraph is logically leaked even though no unsafe code is involved. Replacing the back-edge with Weak removes its contribution to the strong count, so the value collects when its last strong owner drops, and reads go through upgrade(), which returns None once the target is gone. The forward, owning edge stays Rc/Arc; only the observational edge becomes Weak.
